families.s: HSE roof-work planning, access and edge-protection guidance
families.t: planning, competence, safe access, roof edges, openings, sloping and flat roofs, fragile materials and contractor-client coordination
f: All roof work must be organised and planned so that it is carried out safely.
Even roof tasks lasting only a few minutes require proper precautions.
Workers must be trained, competent and instructed in the required precautions.
Safe access may require scaffolds, stair towers, towers, mobile access equipment, secured ladders or roof hatches.
Sloping roofs normally require edge protection and measures to prevent people or materials falling.
Flat-roof edges can be protected by secure double guardrails and toe boards.
Roofs and rooflights should be treated as fragile until a competent person confirms otherwise.
Clients and contractors on business premises should agree how roof-work risks will be managed.
families.g: Roof-work risk depends on roof pitch and condition, edges, openings, fragility, access, weather, duration, materials, rescue arrangements and contractor coordination.

families.s: HSE fragile-roof and fragile-surface control guidance
families.t: assumption of fragility, avoidance, staging, guardrails, restraint, arrest, warning, training and cooperation
f: Work on or near fragile surfaces should be avoided where reasonably practicable.
All roofs should be treated as fragile until a competent person confirms that they are non-fragile.
Rooflights, fibre-cement sheets, corroded metal sheets, glass and deteriorated boards may be fragile.
Where work cannot be avoided, controls may require stagings, guardrails, fall restraint, fall arrest and safety nets.
Precautions are required regardless of how short the work duration is.
Warning notices must identify approaches to fragile surfaces where required.
People doing the work must be trained, competent and instructed in the precautions.
Clients and contractors should cooperate and agree the arrangements before work begins.
families.g: Fragile-surface risk depends on material, age, corrosion, hidden rooflights, loading, access, work position, fall clearance, weather, competence and the combined fall-control system.

families.t: fall mitigation, competent rigging, installation, clearance, inspection, post-fall response, rescue and manufacturer instructions
f: Safety nets and soft-landing systems mitigate fall distance and consequences but do not replace fall prevention.
Safety nets must be installed, modified, maintained and removed by trained competent people.
Nets should be positioned as close as practicable to the working level.
Adequate clearance below a net is required for deformation during fall arrest.
A competent person should inspect the installed system and provide handover evidence.
Safety-net and soft-landing systems require subsequent regular inspection, including weekly checks where specified.
Work should stop after a net arrests a fall until a competent inspection confirms whether it can be reused.
Risk assessments must include rescue and first-aid arrangements for a person caught in a net.
families.g: Fall-mitigation performance depends on system type, rigging, clearance, anchorage, installation height, inspection, environmental damage, rescue and compatibility with the work sequence.

families.s: HSE abrasive-wheel mounting and grinding safety guidance
families.t: wheel selection, speed, inspection, mounting, guarding, training, portable grinders, PPE and maintenance
f: Abrasive-wheel safety depends on matching the wheel characteristics to the machine and intended operation.
Users and people mounting wheels need suitable training for their responsibilities.
The wheel's maximum operating speed must not be exceeded.
Wheels should be inspected for damage and stored and handled to prevent deterioration.
Correct mounting procedures, flanges and blotters are required where applicable.
Grinding machines require suitable guards and work-rest arrangements.
Portable and hand-held grinders require additional control of wheel breakage, kickback, sparks, dust and operator position.
Appropriate eye, face, hearing, respiratory and body protection may be needed after higher-order controls.
families.g: Abrasive-wheel risk depends on wheel type and condition, speed, mounting, machine, guard, workpiece, side loading, environment, operator competence and maintenance.
